title: Climate change, bank liquidity and systemic risk
summary: This ECB working paper examines how climate transition risks affect short-term funding costs in the European repo market using transaction-level data from 2019-2022. The study finds that banks with higher financed emissions (proxy for transition risk exposure) pay 7-12% higher repo rates per one standard deviation increase. This "carbon premium" combines a risk premium and an "inconvenience premium" reflecting dealer bank sustainability preferences. The premium triples during periods of financial stress, indicating climate risks amplify existing vulnerabilities. Additionally, transition risk causes uneven monetary policy transmission, with high-emission banks' repo rates adjusting more quickly to central bank rate hikes.
key_points: Banks with higher financed emissions (GHG of borrowers) pay 7-12% higher repo borrowing rates per one standard deviation increase in transition risk exposure
The carbon premium cannot be explained by collateral quality, transaction maturity, or counterparty relationships
Premium comprises both a risk premium (credit risk compensation) and an "inconvenience premium" (dealer sustainability preferences)
The transition risk premium triples in size during periods of financial stress, amplifying systemic risk
Repo rates for high-emission banks adjust more quickly to ECB rate hikes, indicating uneven monetary policy pass-through
Data covers 46 MMSR-reporting banks with daily transaction volumes EUR 500-1500 billion
why_it_matters: Climate transition risks are already priced into Europe's core bank funding market, creating differentiated borrowing costs based on carbon exposure. This affects bank liquidity availability, financial stability, and the effectiveness of monetary policy transmission. Banks with high financed emissions face structural funding disadvantages that could persist as climate policy tightens. The interaction between climate risks and market stress suggests climate factors could trigger or amplify financial crises.
market_structure_context: The European repo market serves as the backbone of bank liquidity and the primary channel for ECB policy rate transmission. The paper reveals that climate transition risk creates rate segmentation in this market, with carbon-intensive banks paying a persistent premium. This structural friction could impair monetary policy effectiveness if climate risks continue to price unevenly across the banking sector. The "inconvenience premium" component indicates dealer bank sustainability preferences are becoming a market structural factor in short-term funding markets.
important_numbers: 7-12% higher repo rates per one standard deviation increase in financed emissions
Carbon premium triples during financial stress
